groups.sentence: The university vets AI tools and puts data protection measures in place.
Instructors do not require students to enter personal information or original work into AI tools.
Instructors tell students about AI data privacy risks, for example in the syllabus.
Users do not enter confidential, sensitive, personally identifiable or restricted data into AI tools.
Students do not enter personal, confidential or sensitive information into AI tools.
Sensitive or confidential data goes only into AI tools the university has approved, licensed or contractually protected, not public or unapproved ones.
Instructors do not enter student work or identifiable student information into AI tools without student consent or approved tools.
Users check the data's classification and consult the data owner or IT before entering non-public data into AI tools.
Users minimize, anonymize or de-identify data before entering it into AI tools.
Users enter only public information into AI tools, assuming anything entered becomes public; public data may be used freely.
Users opt out of data training, adjust privacy settings and read privacy policies before using AI tools.
Researchers and staff do not enter unpublished research, intellectual property or proprietary material into AI tools.
Instructors do not upload student work to AI detection tools, which may expose student data.
AI tools may store, reuse or train on what users enter, so entered information may not stay private.
Users protect data and privacy and follow university data and privacy policies and laws when using AI.
Entering sensitive data into AI tools can violate FERPA, HIPAA or other privacy rules and expose institutional or student data.
University-approved or licensed AI tools protect entered data and do not use it to train models.
